Set a random seed before each simulation question and report it. You may use standard packages unless a question asks you to write the calculation yourself. Use equal neighbor weights throughout. Here pp counts the covariates used to measure distance; do not add an intercept column to a KNN predictor matrix. R and Python use different random-number generators, so their exact simulation results need not agree.

Question 1: Estimate the bias and variance of KNN

In our previous homework, we used repeated simulations to study the behavior of linear regression estimators. We will now use the same idea for KNN. Consider the regression model

Yi=f(𝑿i)+ϵi,f(𝒙)=0.5x1+sin⁡(x2)−0.3x32, Y_i=f(\mathbf X_i)+\epsilon_i, \qquad f(\mathbf x)=0.5x_1+\sin(x_2)-0.3x_3^2,

where the three covariates are independent standard normal variables and ϵi∼𝒩(0,0.12)\epsilon_i\sim\mathcal N(0,0.1^2) independently of the covariates and other observations. Generate n=400n=400 training observations. Our goal is to estimate the mean response at

𝒙0=(0.5,0.7,1)𝖳. \mathbf x_0=(0.5,0.7,1)^{\mathsf T}.

Use Euclidean distance and consider k=1,3,5,…,29k=1,3,5,\ldots,29.

  1. Calculate f(𝒙0)f(\mathbf x_0). Generate one training dataset and obtain the KNN prediction at 𝒙0\mathbf x_0 for each value of kk.
Show the workflow 
set.seed(432)
n <- 400
x0 <- c(0.5, 0.7, 1)

X <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), nrow = n)
y <- 0.5 * X[, 1] + sin(X[, 2]) - 0.3 * X[, 3]^2 +
     rnorm(n, sd = 0.1)

distance <- sqrt(rowSums(sweep(X, 2, x0, "-")^2))
nearest_y <- y[order(distance)]
k <- seq(1, 29, by = 2)

data.frame(k = k, prediction = cumsum(nearest_y)[k] / k)

The true mean response at (x_0) is (f(x_0)=(0.7)-0.05). For each (k), the KNN prediction is the average response of the (k) training points closest to (x_0).

  1. Independently repeat the generation of the training covariates and responses 200 times. Within each repetition, use the same training data for every value of kk. Store the predictions in a matrix with 200 rows and one column for each value of kk. Use this matrix to estimate the bias, variance, and mean squared error of the estimated mean response. Use divisor 200 when calculating the empirical variance, and verify numerically that

mean squared error=squared bias+variance. \text{mean squared error} =\text{squared bias}+\text{variance}.

Plot squared bias, variance, and mean squared error against kk in one figure. Explain the pattern and compare it with the bias-variance trade-off for ridge regression or lasso.

Show the workflow 
set.seed(432)
n <- 400
B <- 200
k_values <- seq(1, 29, by = 2)
x0 <- c(0.5, 0.7, 1)
true_mean <- sin(0.7) - 0.05

predictions <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = B, ncol = length(k_values))

for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  X <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), nrow = n)
  y <- 0.5 * X[, 1] + sin(X[, 2]) - 0.3 * X[, 3]^2 +
       rnorm(n, sd = 0.1)

  distances <- sqrt(rowSums(sweep(X, 2, x0, "-")^2))
  nearest_y <- y[order(distances)]
  predictions[b, ] <- cumsum(nearest_y)[k_values] / k_values
}

bias <- colMeans(predictions) - true_mean
variance <- colMeans(sweep(predictions, 2, colMeans(predictions), "-")^2)
mse <- colMeans((predictions - true_mean)^2)

results <- data.frame(
  k = k_values,
  bias = bias,
  variance = variance,
  mse = mse
)

I used seed 432 and repeated the simulation 200 times. For each value of (k), I calculated the bias, variance, and mean squared error (MSE) of the KNN predictions. The results confirm that MSE equals squared bias plus variance.

Question 2: Compare KNN with lasso

Use the response model from Question 1, including the noise standard deviation 0.10.1, but generate p=30p=30 covariates. The response still depends only on the first three. Consider these two settings:

  • Setting 1: all 30 covariates are independent standard normal variables.

  • Setting 2: the covariates have a multivariate normal distribution with mean zero and covariance matrix 𝚺\boldsymbol\Sigma, where

    Σjj=1,Σjl=0.8for j≠l. \Sigma_{jj}=1, \qquad \Sigma_{jl}=0.8\quad\text{for }j\ne l.

In each setting, generate 400 training observations and 1,000 independent test observations. Fit 5NN using Euclidean distance on the supplied covariate scale. All covariates already have population variance one.

For lasso, use a linear model containing the 30 covariates and a separately fitted, unpenalized intercept. Follow the Week 4 objective,

Lλ(𝜷)=12n∥𝒚̃−𝑿𝜷∥22+λ‖𝜷‖1, L_\lambda(\boldsymbol\beta) =\frac{1}{2n}\left\lVert \widetilde{\mathbf y}-\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta \right\rVert_2^2 +\lambda\lVert\boldsymbol\beta\rVert_1,

where 𝑿∈ℝn×30\mathbf X\in\mathbb R^{n\times30} contains the centered and standardized covariates and 𝒚̃\widetilde{\mathbf y} is the centered training response. Select the penalty by ten-fold cross-validation over 41 logarithmically spaced values from 10−410^{-4} to 11. Estimate all means and scales using only the training portion of each fold, with divisor equal to that portion’s sample size. After selecting the penalty, refit on all training observations and apply the fitted transformations unchanged to the test observations. Do not add nonlinear terms to the lasso model.

  1. Fit both methods in each setting. Use the same training and test data for the two methods within a setting. Report their test MSE values in one table, together with the selected lasso penalty and the number of nonzero lasso slopes. You only need to generate one dataset for each setting; repeated simulations are not required.
Show the workflow 
library(glmnet)
Loading required package: Matrix
Loaded glmnet 5.0
Show the workflow 
set.seed(433)  # Simulation seed

p <- 30
lambda <- 10^seq(-4, 0, length.out = 41)

run <- function(correlated) {
  make_x <- function(n) {
    Z <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
    if (correlated) sqrt(0.8) * rnorm(n) + sqrt(0.2) * Z else Z
  }
  make_y <- function(X) {
    0.5 * X[, 1] + sin(X[, 2]) - 0.3 * X[, 3]^2 +
      rnorm(nrow(X), sd = 0.1)
  }

  X <- make_x(400); y <- make_y(X)
  Xtest <- make_x(1000); ytest <- make_y(Xtest)

  knn <- apply(Xtest, 1, function(x) {
    d <- rowSums(sweep(X, 2, x, "-")^2)
    mean(y[order(d)[1:5]])
  })

  cv <- cv.glmnet(X, y, lambda = lambda, nfolds = 10)
  fit <- glmnet(X, y, lambda = lambda)
  selected <- cv$lambda.min
  lasso <- as.numeric(predict(fit, Xtest, s = selected))

  data.frame(
    setting = if (correlated) "Correlated" else "Independent",
    KNN_MSE = mean((ytest - knn)^2),
    lasso_MSE = mean((ytest - lasso)^2),
    lambda = selected,
    nonzero_slopes = sum(as.numeric(coef(fit, s = selected))[-1] != 0)
  )
}

rbind(run(FALSE), run(TRUE))
      setting   KNN_MSE lasso_MSE     lambda nonzero_slopes
1 Independent 0.5274034 0.2426440 0.03162278              8
2  Correlated 0.1961747 0.3113866 0.01995262              8

Using seed 433, I fit 5NN and lasso in both settings and compared their test MSEs. The table also shows the selected lasso penalty and the number of nonzero slopes.

  1. Compare the results between the two settings. Explain how correlation can change the usefulness of Euclidean neighborhoods, and why lasso does not use all covariates in the same way as KNN.

When the covariates are correlated, nearby points under Euclidean distance may have more similar values of the important covariates, which can help KNN. Lasso uses the covariates as separate predictors, so it can give small or zero coefficients to less useful ones. The test MSEs in the table show how these effects worked in this simulation.

  1. The response model contains sin⁡(X2)\sin(X_2) and X32X_3^2, but the lasso fit uses only linear terms. Explain how this difference affects the comparison. Would the results justify a general claim that correlation always helps KNN, or that one method is always better? Explain why.

The true response includes ((X_2)) and (X_3^2), but the lasso model uses only linear terms. Lasso therefore cannot represent the true relationship exactly. KNN can capture these nonlinear patterns, though using all 30 covariates to find neighbors may hurt its predictions. These results do not show that correlation always helps KNN or that either method is always better.

Question 3: Observed dimension and latent dimension

The lecture’s handwritten digit example shows that KNN can work with many measured covariates. We will use a simulation to investigate why the structure of those covariates matters.

Let p=100p=100 be the number of observed covariates and let mm be the number of latent variables. For each observation, generate

𝑿i=𝑨𝒁i+𝜼i,Yi=Zi1+Zi2+ϵi, \mathbf X_i=\mathbf A\mathbf Z_i+\boldsymbol\eta_i, \qquad Y_i=Z_{i1}+Z_{i2}+\epsilon_i,

where 𝑨∈ℝ100×m\mathbf A\in\mathbb R^{100\times m} has independent entries from Uniform[−2,2][-2,2]. The entries of 𝒁i∈ℝm\mathbf Z_i\in\mathbb R^m and 𝜼i∈ℝ100\boldsymbol\eta_i\in\mathbb R^{100}, and the scalar ϵi\epsilon_i, are independent standard normal variables, also independent of 𝑨\mathbf A. Generate 𝑨\mathbf A once and use it for all training and test observations in that dataset.

Compare m=3m=3 and m=30m=30. In each setting, generate 200 training observations and 200 independent test observations. Fit KNN using only the 100 observed covariates in 𝑿\mathbf X, with Euclidean distance on their generated scale. The latent variables in 𝒁\mathbf Z are used to generate the data but are not available to the fitted model. Consider k=2,10,18,…,82k=2,10,18,\ldots,82.

  1. Generate one dataset for each value of mm. Fit KNN for every value of kk and calculate test MSE. Within a setting, use the same training and test observations for all values of kk.
Show the workflow 
set.seed(434)
k_values <- seq(2, 82, by = 8)

run_setting <- function(m) {
  A <- matrix(runif(100 * m, -2, 2), 100, m)

  make_data <- function(n) {
    Z <- matrix(rnorm(n * m), n, m)
    X <- Z %*% t(A) + matrix(rnorm(n * 100), n, 100)
    y <- Z[, 1] + Z[, 2] + rnorm(n)
    list(X = X, y = y)
  }

  train <- make_data(200)
  test <- make_data(200)

  distances <- outer(
    rowSums(train$X^2), rowSums(test$X^2), "+"
  ) - 2 * tcrossprod(train$X, test$X)

  predictions <- apply(distances, 2, function(d) {
    nearest_y <- train$y[order(d, seq_along(d))]
    cumsum(nearest_y)[k_values] / k_values
  })

  data.frame(
    m = m,
    k = k_values,
    test_MSE = rowMeans(
      sweep(predictions, 2, test$y, "-")^2
    )
  )
}

results_3a <- rbind(run_setting(3), run_setting(30))

  1. Repeat the complete experiment 50 times, generating a new 𝑨\mathbf A and new observations in each repetition. Plot average test MSE against kk, with one curve for each value of mm. These curves compare the specified choices of kk in a controlled simulation; they are not a cross-validation procedure for selecting a final model.
Show the workflow 
set.seed(435)  # Simulation seed

simulations <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:50, function(rep) {
  rbind(run_setting(3), run_setting(30))
}))

average_mse <- aggregate(test_MSE ~ m + k, simulations, mean)

m3 <- subset(average_mse, m == 3)
m30 <- subset(average_mse, m == 30)

plot(m3$k, m3$test_MSE, type = "b", col = "blue", pch = 16,
     ylim = range(average_mse$test_MSE),
     xlab = "k", ylab = "Average test MSE")
lines(m30$k, m30$test_MSE, type = "b", col = "red", pch = 17)
legend("topright", c("m = 3", "m = 30"),
       col = c("blue", "red"), pch = c(16, 17), lty = 1)

I repeated the experiment 50 times, generating a new matrix (A) and new observations each time. The plot shows the average test MSE for each (k). These (k) values were specified for comparison; I did not use cross-validation to select a final model.

  1. Both settings have 100 observed covariates, and the response depends on only two latent variables. Explain why their KNN performance can still differ. What role does the noise 𝜼i\boldsymbol\eta_i play, and why are the observed data not confined exactly to an mm-dimensional linear space?

KNN can perform differently because Euclidean distance uses all 100 observed variables, while the response depends on only two latent variables. With (m=30), the observations contain more latent variation unrelated to the response, so nearby points may have less similar responses. The noise (_i) also affects distances, and the observed variables do not lie exactly in an (m)-dimensional linear space.

Question 4: Classify handwritten digits

Use zip.train and zip.test from the R package ElemStatLearn, as in the lecture. The package has been retired from the active CRAN repository. If needed, install the archived package into your usual R library, then load the two datasets. Python users can obtain the same training data and test data directly from the book’s authors; these are whitespace-separated files without headers.

Each image has 16×16=25616\times16=256 pixel values. The first column is the digit label and the remaining columns are the pixel values. Use the first 1,000 rows of zip.train and the first 500 rows of zip.test. Use the original pixel values without standardization, and do not include the digit label in a distance calculation.

For a test image 𝒙0\mathbf x_0 and a training image 𝒙i\mathbf x_i, the two distances are

dE(𝒙0,𝒙i)=∑j=1256(x0j−xij)2,dM(𝒙0,𝒙i)=∑j=1256|x0j−xij|. d_E(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf x_i) =\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{256}(x_{0j}-x_{ij})^2}, \qquad d_M(\mathbf x_0,\mathbf x_i) =\sum_{j=1}^{256}|x_{0j}-x_{ij}|.

  1. Write a 5NN classification function that allows either Euclidean or Manhattan distance. For each test image, calculate its distances to the training images directly, find the five nearest, and return the most frequent digit label. Break distance ties by the smaller training row number and voting ties by the smallest digit. Do not use a built-in distance or KNN function for this part.
Show the workflow 
classify_5nn <- function(train_x, train_y, test_x,
                         distance = "euclidean") {
  differences <- sweep(train_x, 2, test_x, "-")

  if (distance == "euclidean") {
    d <- sqrt(rowSums(differences^2))
  } else if (distance == "manhattan") {
    d <- rowSums(abs(differences))
  } else {
    stop("Distance must be 'euclidean' or 'manhattan'.")
  }

  nearest <- order(d, seq_along(d))[1:5]
  votes <- tabulate(as.integer(train_y[nearest]) + 1, nbins = 10)
  which.max(votes) - 1
}

The function calculates the distance from a test image to every training image, finds the five nearest images, and predicts the most common digit. Ties in distance use the smaller training row number; ties in votes use the smaller digit.

  1. Apply the classifier to all 500 test images using each distance. For each fit, report the test classification error and a 10×1010\times10 confusion matrix, with rows representing predicted digits and columns representing true digits. Keep all digit labels from 0 through 9 in the matrix, including any with a zero count. Which digits are most often confused with one another?
Show the workflow 
train_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".gz")
test_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".gz")

download.file(
  "https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/datasets/zip.train.gz",
  train_file, mode = "wb"
)
download.file(
  "https://hastie.su.domains/ElemStatLearn/datasets/zip.test.gz",
  test_file, mode = "wb"
)

zip.train <- read.table(gzfile(train_file, "rt"), header = FALSE)
zip.test <- read.table(gzfile(test_file, "rt"), header = FALSE)
Show the workflow 
train <- zip.train[1:1000, ]
test <- zip.test[1:500, ]
train_x <- as.matrix(train[, -1])
test_x <- as.matrix(test[, -1])
train_y <- train[, 1]
test_y <- test[, 1]

all_x <- rbind(train_x, test_x)

euclidean <- as.matrix(
  dist(all_x, method = "euclidean")
)[1:1000, 1001:1500]

manhattan <- as.matrix(
  dist(all_x, method = "manhattan")
)[1:1000, 1001:1500]

predict_5nn <- function(distances) {
  apply(distances, 2, function(d) {
    nearest <- order(d, seq_along(d))[1:5]
    votes <- tabulate(as.integer(train_y[nearest]) + 1, nbins = 10)
    which.max(votes) - 1
  })
}

pred_e <- predict_5nn(euclidean)
pred_m <- predict_5nn(manhattan)

for (name in c("Euclidean", "Manhattan")) {
  pred <- if (name == "Euclidean") pred_e else pred_m
  cat("\n", name, "test error:", mean(pred != test_y), "\n")
  print(table(
    Predicted = factor(pred, levels = 0:9),
    True = factor(test_y, levels = 0:9)
  ))
}

Question 5: Create a plot-formatting skill

Create a short SKILL.md file for improving the formatting of STAT 432 homework plots. You may use AI to help write it.

  1. Include a title, a description, and a few formatting rules. The description should limit the skill to STAT 432 homework plot improvements and require an explicit request to use it. Your rules should address margins, titles, axes, labels, colors, and sizes for plots produced in R or Python. Keep them portable: do not refer to specific homework questions.

  2. Ask your agent to install the skill. Explicitly call it to improve the plot from Question 1, then compare the original and revised versions. Do you like the changes? You may revise the skill and test it a couple more times, or uninstall it if it remains unhelpful.

I prefer the revised plot because the title and axis labels are clearer. The different colors and marker shapes make the three curves easier to compare.

  1. Append your final SKILL.md content to your submission and briefly explain your choices and experience.

My final SKILL.md is:

---
name: stat432-plot-formatting
description: Improve the formatting of STAT 432 homework plots in R or Python only when the user explicitly requests this skill.
---

# STAT 432 Plot Formatting

Improve plot readability while preserving the data and calculations.

- Margins: Leave enough space so titles, labels, and legends are not cut off.
- Titles: Use a short, descriptive title.
- Axes: Use readable tick marks and consistent scales when comparing plots.
- Labels: Clearly name each axis and include units when relevant.
- Colors: Use a colorblind-friendly palette and distinguish curves with line styles or markers.
- Sizes: Start with a 7-by-5-inch figure and 12-point text; adjust as needed for readability.
- Legends: Place legends where they do not cover important data.
- Check: Render the revised plot and inspect it for overlapping or clipped text.

I chose these rules to make my plots easier to read. I preferred the revised plot because the labels were clearer and the colors and marker shapes made the curves easier to compare. Checking the rendered plot also helped fix overlapping legend labels.
